subject: chem
title: Group 17 (Halogens)
subtitle: Properties, reactions and trends of the halogens.
concept: Halogens become less reactive (weaker oxidising agents) down the group as electronegativity and electron affinity decrease.
Halogen displacement reactions demonstrate relative oxidising power; solvent extraction with cyclohexane identifies products.
Hydrogen halides (HX) dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids; their thermal stability decreases down the group.

notes.heading: Physical Properties
items: F₂: pale yellow gas. Cl₂: yellow-green gas. Br₂: orange-brown liquid. I₂: grey-black solid/purple vapour.
Boiling points increase down the group: larger molecules → stronger id-id intermolecular forces.
Electronegativity: F > Cl > Br > I (decreases down group).
Oxidising power (E°): F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

notes.heading: Reactions of Halogens
items: With metals: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl; Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂ (halides formed).
With water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl (chloric(I) acid, weak acid, bleaching). I₂ very slightly soluble.
Disproportionation: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O (bleach). Hot conc. NaOH: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O.
Displacement: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂; Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂. Bromine displaces iodide but not chloride.

notes.heading: Hydrogen Halides
items: HF, HCl, HBr, HI: all colourless gases; dissolve in water to form acids.
HF is a weak acid (H-bonds very strong); HCl, HBr, HI are strong acids.
Thermal stability: HF > HCl > HBr > HI (bond enthalpy decreases down group).

Reaction of NaX with H₂SO₄: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (works for Cl only). NaBr + H₂SO₄ → HBr + SO₂ (HBr oxidised by H₂SO₄); NaI: HI + I₂ + H₂S (I⁻ is strong enough reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄ to H₂S).

definitions.body: A reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
The ability of a halogen to accept electrons (be reduced); decreases down Group 17.
Decreases down Group 17 as the H–X bond enthalpy decreases; HI decomposes most easily on heating.

workedExamples.q: Bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution, then cyclohexane is added and the mixture shaken. Describe and explain the observations.

steps.text: Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂. Bromine (better oxidising agent) displaces iodide ions.
Orange-brown Br₂ is decolourised; I₂ produced gives a brown colour to aqueous layer.
I₂ is more soluble in non-polar cyclohexane → cyclohexane layer turns violet/purple.

mistakes: Stating that bromine cannot displace chloride — correct! Bromine can only displace iodide (Br₂ is less reactive than Cl₂).
Forgetting to describe BOTH layers (aqueous and cyclohexane) in solvent extraction tests.
Confusing 'disproportionation' with 'displacement' — in disproportionation, the SAME element is both oxidised and reduced.
tips: Cyclohexane layer colours: Cl₂ → pale yellow; Br₂ → orange; I₂ → violet/purple.
H₂SO₄ reactions: NaCl → only HCl gas (no redox); NaBr → HBr + SO₂ (Br⁻ reduces S); NaI → HI + S/SO₂/H₂S (I⁻ stronger reducer).
Thermal stability order: HF > HCl > HBr > HI — parallel to bond enthalpy order.

flashcards.q: State the trend in oxidising power of halogens.
flashcards.a: Decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (electronegativity and electron affinity decrease).
A reaction where the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced (e.g. Cl₂ in NaOH solution).

flashcards.q: What is the observation when Cl₂ is added to KI(aq) and then cyclohexane?
flashcards.a: Aqueous layer turns brown (I₂); cyclohexane (upper) layer turns violet/purple (I₂ more soluble in organic layer).

flashcards.q: Why is HI less thermally stable than HCl?
flashcards.a: The H–I bond enthalpy is lower than H–Cl; less energy is needed to break H–I, so HI decomposes more easily on heating.

flashcards.q: Why does NaI + H₂SO₄ produce H₂S but NaCl + H₂SO₄ does not?
flashcards.a: I⁻ is a stronger reducing agent than Cl⁻; it can reduce H₂SO₄ all the way to H₂S. Cl⁻ cannot reduce H₂SO₄.

flashcards.q: What forms when Cl₂ dissolves in water?
flashcards.a: HCl + HOCl (chloric(I) acid / hypochlorous acid); HOCl is a bleaching agent (oxidises dyes).

questions.q: Which halogen is the strongest oxidising agent?
questions.exp: F₂ has the highest electronegativity and electron affinity → strongest oxidising agent; E°(F₂/F⁻) = +2.87 V.

questions.q: What is observed when bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution?
opts: No reaction — Br₂ cannot displace Cl⁻
questions.exp: Br₂ is a weaker oxidising agent than Cl₂ and cannot displace Cl⁻ from solution — no reaction.

questions.q: Cl₂ reacts with NaOH solution to give NaCl and NaOCl. What type of reaction is this?
questions.exp: Disproportionation: Cl is oxidised (0 → +1 in NaOCl) and reduced (0 → −1 in NaCl) simultaneously.

questions.q: NaI is reacted with concentrated H₂SO₄. What gas with characteristic smell is produced?
questions.exp: I⁻ is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄ all the way to H₂S (rotten eggs). HI is also produced initially.

questions.q: Which colour does iodine give in cyclohexane?
questions.exp: I₂ dissolved in cyclohexane gives a characteristic violet/purple colour.

questions.q: Which halogen is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.exp: Bromine (Br₂) is the only halogen that is liquid at room temperature (melting point −7 °C, boiling point 59 °C). F₂ and Cl₂ are gases; I₂ is a solid.

questions.q: Cl₂ is bubbled into KBr solution. What is observed?
opts: No reaction — Cl₂ is less reactive than Br₂
The solution turns orange-brown — Br₂ is displaced
questions.exp: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so it displaces bromide ions from solution. The liberated Br₂ gives the characteristic orange-brown colour.

questions.q: What is produced when concentrated H₂SO₄ is added to NaI?
questions.exp: I⁻ is a stronger reducing agent than Br⁻ or Cl⁻. It reduces H₂SO₄ all the way: SO₄²⁻ → SO₂ → S → H₂S. Products include HI, SO₂, S, and H₂S (steamy fumes + yellow solid + bad smell).

questions.q: Why does HF have a much higher boiling point than HCl despite lower Mr?
opts: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
questions.exp: F is the most electronegative element; H–F bonds are highly polar, allowing strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. This raises the boiling point of HF far above what its Mr would predict.

questions.q: Which test distinguishes Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻ in solution?
opts: Adding dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃ — different AgX precipitate colours and solubilities in NH₃
Adding Cl₂ water and shaking with cyclohexane
questions.exp: Adding acidified AgNO₃: Cl⁻ → white AgCl (soluble in dilute NH₃); Br⁻ → cream AgBr (soluble in conc NH₃); I⁻ → yellow AgI (insoluble in NH₃). The precipitate colour and NH₃ solubility together confirm the identity.

questions.q: The oxidising power of halogens decreases down Group 17. Which explains this?
opts: Atomic radius decreases, so attraction for electrons decreases
Atomic radius increases, so the incoming electron is less strongly attracted to the nucleus
Ionic radius decreases down the group
questions.exp: Larger atoms have more electron shielding and greater atomic radius. The nucleus exerts less attraction on an incoming electron, so the tendency to be reduced (gain electrons) decreases — oxidising power falls.

questions.q: What colour does iodine give in hexane (cyclohexane) extraction?
questions.exp: Iodine dissolves readily in non-polar hexane/cyclohexane, giving a characteristic violet/purple colour. This distinguishes it from Br₂ (orange) and Cl₂ (pale yellow) in the same solvent.

questions.q: Fluorine does not undergo disproportionation in NaOH because:
opts: It has no d-orbitals and cannot be oxidised further (it has no +ve oxidation states)
It reacts with NaOH too slowly
questions.exp: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and has no available d-orbitals. It cannot exhibit positive oxidation states, so it cannot disproportionate (unlike Cl₂, which gives Cl⁻ and ClO⁻ in NaOH).

questions.q: Silver iodide (AgI) is described as 'insoluble in ammonia solution'. What does this mean for the silver halide test?
opts: AgI gives no precipitate with AgNO₃
AgI is the cream precipitate (confused with AgBr)
Adding NH₃ to AgI precipitate does not dissolve it — confirming I⁻
questions.exp: AgI is yellow and insoluble in both dilute and concentrated ammonia. This contrasts with AgCl (dissolves in dilute NH₃) and AgBr (dissolves only in concentrated NH₃), completing the three-way identification.

questions.q: What is the role of the Fe catalyst in the reaction of Cl₂ with benzene (electrophilic substitution)?
opts: It is oxidised by Cl₂ to Fe³⁺, which acts as a Lewis acid catalyst generating Cl⁺
It increases the concentration of Cl₂
It acts as a Brønsted base
questions.exp: Fe + Cl₂ → FeCl₃. FeCl₃ is a Lewis acid that accepts a lone pair from Cl₂: Cl₂ + FeCl₃ → Cl⁺ + FeCl₄⁻. The Cl⁺ electrophile then attacks the benzene ring.

questions.q: Which halogen is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.exp: Bromine (Br₂) is the only halogen that is liquid at room temperature (bp 59°C).

questions.q: Why does the boiling point increase down Group 17?
opts: Larger molecules with stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces
questions.exp: Larger electron clouds in heavier halogens produce stronger id–id (van der Waals) forces, requiring more energy to vaporise.

questions.q: Chlorine water reacts with cold NaOH to produce:
questions.exp: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. This disproportionation produces both Cl⁻ (−1) and ClO⁻ (+1).

questions.q: In the test for halide ions using AgNO₃, which precipitate dissolves in dilute NH₃?
questions.exp: White AgCl dissolves in dilute NH₃ to form [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. AgBr dissolves only in concentrated NH₃; AgI is insoluble in NH₃.

questions.q: NaBr reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄. Which gases are produced?
questions.exp: Br⁻ is a stronger reducing agent than Cl⁻. It reduces H₂SO₄: HBr is produced, and H₂SO₄ is partially reduced to SO₂.

questions.q: Which halogen has the highest electronegativity?
questions.exp: Fluorine is the most electronegative element (Pauling scale: 4.0), due to its small atomic radius and high nuclear charge.

questions.q: Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ from solution. This shows:
opts: Cl₂ is a weaker oxidising agent than Br₂
Cl₂ is a stronger oxidising agent than Br₂
Br₂ is more reactive than Cl₂
questions.exp: A more reactive (stronger oxidising) halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution. Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ in oxidising power.

questions.q: What colour does iodine give in an organic solvent (cyclohexane) layer?
questions.exp: I₂ dissolved in non-polar cyclohexane gives a characteristic violet/purple colour.

questions.q: Why is HF a weaker acid than HCl despite F being more electronegative?
opts: F–H bond is stronger and harder to break
F is too small to ionise
questions.exp: The H–F bond is very strong (bond enthalpy ~570 kJ mol⁻¹), so ionisation is less favourable than in HCl (~432 kJ mol⁻¹).

questions.q: Fluorine does not show positive oxidation states. Why?
opts: It has no d orbitals and is the most electronegative element
questions.exp: F has no vacant d orbitals for expansion of the valence shell and, being the most electronegative element, never acts as the less electronegative partner.

recall: State and explain the trend in oxidising power of halogens.
Describe and explain the displacement reactions of halogens.
Describe the reactions of Na halides with H₂SO₄ and explain the differences.
Explain what disproportionation means and give an example.
Describe the solvent extraction test using cyclohexane.

summary.label: Displacement
summary.value: more reactive halogen displaces less reactive halide

summary.label: Cyclohexane colours
summary.value: Cl₂ pale yellow; Br₂ orange; I₂ violet

summary.label: Disproportionation
summary.value: Cl₂ + NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl (Cl oxidised and reduced)
